activities.anchor: he left gaps for elements nobody had found yet
activities.caption: put the three confirmations in order — the predictions came true on schedule
activities.name: ptGapOrder

config.prompt: Three discoveries arrived to fill the 1869 prediction spaces — put them in the order they were found:
config.why: Predicted properties confirmed by discovery is what turned a sorting exercise into chemistry's foundation.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — how much each level holds
activities.name: ptShellCloze

config.text: Moving left to right across any period, the same outer level fills up: period 1's level holds %%0%%, periods 2 and 3 hold %%1%% each, and from period 4 onward it holds %%2%%.
config.hint: The row lengths in the lesson are 2, then 8, then 8, then 18 — the capacities do the setting.

activities.caption: file six elements by their column
activities.name: ptFamilySort

config.prompt: Sort each element into its column: I, VII or VIII (0).
config.why: Same outer-count, same conduct: column I hands its lone outer electron away, column VII grabs one, column VIII wants none at all.

activities.anchor: they would rather do almost anything
activities.caption: slide to the melting point of the bottom alkali metal
activities.name: ptCsPlace

config.prompt: Caesium sits at the bottom of column I. Slide the marker to its melting point.
config.why: Caesium melts at just 28.5 °C — on a warm day it is literally liquid metal. Lithium, at the top, holds out until 181 °C.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the water demo, retold
activities.name: ptWaterSpot

config.prompt: A student retells the group-I water demonstration. One line is wrong — click it:
lines: A pea-sized piece of sodium skims the water surface, fizzing hard.
The reaction releases hydrogen gas and leaves an alkaline hydroxide: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.
Lithium fizzes gently, sodium ignites with a yellow-orange flame, potassium burns lilac.
Rubidium and caesium are calmer than potassium — past potassium, extra shielding makes the outer electron harder to lose.
That is why sodium is stored under oil: to keep air and moisture away.
config.correction: Rubidium and caesium detonate on contact — each new shielding level makes the outer electron EASIER to lose, so reactivity keeps climbing down the column.
config.why: Shielding does not calm things down: more full levels between nucleus and outer electron means it is lost ever more easily.

activities.caption: pair each halogen clash with its outcome
activities.name: ptDispMatch

config.prompt: Pair each halogen clash with its outcome — only the hungrier element wins:

pairs.left: chlorine gas bubbled through potassium bromide solution
pairs.right: the solution turns orange — bromine is pushed out

pairs.left: bromine dripped into potassium chloride solution
pairs.right: nothing happens — bromine cannot displace chloride
the top electron-grabber always takes it

config.why: To react, a halogen must pull an electron in; as atoms gain levels the incoming electron feels an ever more distant, shielded nucleus — so Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂ runs one way only.

activities.anchor: The two families bracket the table's appetite
activities.caption: drag the divider — one column gives, the other takes
activities.name: ptJawsCompare

config.prompt: Reactivity down the columns — drag the divider across the two edges of the table:

before.label: column I, going down
before.text: Losing the lone outer electron gets easier as shielding grows — lithium fizzes, sodium flares, potassium ignites, caesium detonates.

after.label: column VII, going down
after.text: Gaining an electron gets harder as the incoming one feels a more distant, shielded nucleus — fluorine violent, chlorine fierce, bromine moderate, iodine tame.

config.why: Same shielding geometry, opposite directions: one edge hands electrons away, the other pulls them in.

activities.caption: which curve is atomic radius across a period?
activities.name: ptRadiusTrace

config.prompt: Atomic radius plotted against position across a period (1 = left edge, 7 = right edge) — which curve is right?
config.why: Extra protons pull every outer charge harder while new ones join the same level, so radius falls left to right. Going DOWN a column shows the opposite jump, as whole new levels stack on.
